recent_posts.topic_title: QuotaCell: Let your team spend without handing over the treasury
recent_posts.author: Ticoworld
recent_posts.content_text:
QuotaCell progress: Owner revocation and treasury recovery now tested on CKB
In my previous update, I shared how QuotaCell enforces shared spending limits through CKB scripts.
This week, I focused on another important question: Can a treasury owner revoke delegated access and recover the protected funds without relying on the delegates?
I’ve now tested the owner-control lifecycle using real signed transactions on a fresh isolated CKB node, without modifying the existing policy.
The results:
Revocation: An owner-signed transaction revoked a delegate’s authority and committed successfully.
Enforcement: A newly signed payment using the updated policy state reached the node and was rejected at Q17 because the delegate was disabled. This was not a stale-Cell rejection.
Treasury recovery: The owner closed the policy and recovered all 200 protected synthetic tokens, along with the fund Cell’s 154 CKB capacity, into an owner-controlled token Cell. No delegate signature was required.
Recovery after closure: I deposited 50 of those same tokens back into the protected treasury after closure. The policy remained CLOSED, and a separate owner-signed sweep successfully recovered the deposit.
The final owner balance remained 200 tokens, since the late deposit reused previously recovered funds.
An important limitation also became clear in the executed lifecycle.
The current policy retains all 600 CKB of its policy Cell after closure, with an occupied minimum of approximately 572 CKB. That capacity isn’t a transaction fee, but it remains unavailable for reuse under this experimental design.
The recovered fund capacity is also held in owner-controlled typed token Cells, not automatically converted into freely spendable CKB.
This is still an experimental implementation using synthetic xUDT on a local CKB node. It isn’t a public-testnet release, independent reproduction or a security audit.
The broader goal is to make shared spending authority practical for CKB teams and applications, with enforceable delegation, owner control, recovery and reusable integration components.
The new signed transaction evidence, capacity accounting, validation tools and reproduction instructions are now public:

# Reproduce owner revocation and recovery
Use Windows and a **new disposable checkout**. Existing runners generate test
keys, a local chain and new results; do not run them in a preserved evidence
checkout. Prerequisites: Python 3, Node/npm and the WSL Ubuntu Clang 18 / Linux
LLD 22.1.8 setup in [BUILD_AND_TEST.md](../../docs/BUILD_AND_TEST.md). The
recorded runtime is in [environment.json](environment.json). Cargo is needed
for the optional full 89-case verifier replay, not this owner node test.
```powershell
git clone --config core.autocrlf=false https://github.com/Ticoworld/QuotaCell.git QuotaCell-owner-replay
Set-Location QuotaCell-owner-replay
python -B scripts/acquire_replay_dependencies.py --rpc-url https://testnet.ckb.dev/
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Dependency acquisition failed' }
python -B policy/build_q.py
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Q build failed' }
Push-Location examples/local-chain
npm.cmd ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Locked npm install failed' }
Pop-Location
This file has been truncated. show original
The next challenges are making owner recovery independently usable, improving the policy’s capital efficiency and supporting practical native CKB payments.

recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @NOrththebear,
Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the Bees Network proposal.
After review by the Spark Program Committee, your proposal is currently Pending. This is not a rejection; rather, we invite you to revise your proposal.
The Committee has two main questions:
Reward pool funding and economic model: The Committee would like to understand where the reward pool’s funding comes from. Specifically, please explain how the economic model works: who funds the rewards, how the reward pool is replenished, and what sustainable source funds incentives for observation service providers.
Verifying the authenticity of observations: The Committee has concerns about the reliability of the current verification mechanism. Wallet signatures, Merkle proofs, and on-chain claim transactions can prove that a task was claimed and its results submitted, but they cannot prove that the observation was actually conducted from the claimed network location. Please explain how you ensure that observations are authentic.
Please revise and resubmit your proposal based on this feedback. We will arrange another review as soon as possible.
Best regards
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | Bees Network — Decentralized Observation Layer for AI Agents on CKB
recent_posts.author: NOrththebear
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @xingtianchunyan
Thank you for the review and the clear feedback. We have revised the proposal with two new sections — §6 Economic Model (reward funding) and §7 Observation Authenticity — and resubmitted it. Short answers:
1) Who funds the rewards, and how is the pool replenished?
The testnet rewards today are bootstrapped from the project’s own operator treasury. That is a development subsidy, not the long-term model, and we say so plainly in the revised proposal.
The sustainable source is demand-side payment. AI-agent developers and data teams buy observations from the network (prepaid credits or per-call), paying in RUSD, a CKB-native stablecoin (sUDT), so prices are stable while settlement stays on CKB (testnet RUSD during beta; mainnet confirmed at launch. We use an x402-compatible 402 Payment Required handshake (quote, pay, retry with receipt) but settle in RUSD on CKB through our own verifier — x402’s published facilitators do not support CKB. Each payment is split into a provider reward pool (75%) and a protocol/operations fee (25%). The coordinator sizes each epoch’s budget from actual inflow — capped, with a reserve floor — and distributes it pro-rata to verified points. Rewards therefore come out of revenue, not inflation: there is no token sale and no fixed yield. If revenue is low, rewards scale down rather than being promised. Node stake is CKB or RUSD; no network token is required.
During the beta, a capped treasury budget plus valueless testnet CKB funds the pilot. The $2,000 grant covers engineering and beta costs, not the reward pool itself. The dashboard will publish inflow, epoch budget, and payouts so the model is auditable.
2) How do we know an observation was really made from the claimed location?
We are explicit that no scheme can cryptographically prove physical network location. Instead we add layered, probabilistic and economic assurance:
Replication + quorum: every task is sent to k≥3 independent nodes; only quorum-agreed results are paid.
Hidden canaries: tasks with known ground truth continuously measure each node’s accuracy; low-accuracy nodes lose eligibility.
Diversity: quorum members must differ in ASN / IP prefix / geography, with per-operator caps to resist Sybil clusters.
Signed evidence bundles: nonce, response/header hashes, TLS certificate fingerprint, DNS answers and timing are checked for internal consistency and plausibility.
Stake + slashing: nodes stake CKB, with a dispute window before payout and slashing for proven fraud.
Consumer-side confidence: each observation carries an explicit confidence score, and buyers can pay for more replicas or more diverse vantage points.
This mirrors how crowdsourced measurement networks (RIPE Atlas, Grass) establish trust — replication, canaries and reputation rather than a location proof — and the proposal states that limit openly rather than overclaiming.
The revised 8-week plan adds quorum verification, canaries, and staking to the scope, with accuracy and disagreement metrics published in the beta report.

JoyID testnet: a supported path for headless CI testing
I’m documenting this Light dApp Kit integration blocker here because JoyID’s feedback link is unavailable.
The goal is to cover the JoyID testnet connect flow through @ckb-ccc/joy-id in automated regression tests.
What the investigation found
The 2026-10-28 investigation used headless Chromium on Linux with a CDP virtual authenticator against https://testnet.joyid.dev/auth. The reported diagnostic sequence was:
The popup keeps window.opener when the dApp uses Document-Isolation-Policy: isolate-and-require-corp.
With the virtual authenticator attached, the platform-authenticator availability check returns true, and navigator.credentials.create() succeeds.
JoyID then displays “JoyID is not supported in current environment”, asking for Chrome 130 or later with Google Account sync.
The investigation points to the client-side isSupportedPasskey() AAGUID allow-list check, rather than a failure to create a WebAuthn credential. Chrome’s virtual authenticator reports 01020304-0506-0708-0102-030405060708, which is not an accepted provider in this flow.
This blocks the current headless test setup even though passkey creation succeeds. Relying on a signed-in consumer password-manager account would also make CI provisioning and new-device verification considerably more involved.
What would help
Preferred: an explicit testnet-only flag that relaxes the AAGUID allow-list for automated testing, honored only on testnet.joyid.dev.
Accept Chrome’s virtual-authenticator AAGUID on testnet.
Provide a documented test harness or supported mock for JoyID connect/sign integration tests.
The request is strictly for testnet testing support, with production behavior unchanged.
Reproduction
Serve the dApp with the isolation header above, open JoyID through the CCC connector, attach a CDP virtual authenticator to the navigated JoyID popup, then choose Create New. Passkey creation succeeds, but JoyID rejects the environment before the connection completes.
Playwright test and CDP configuration
Could a JoyID maintainer advise on a supported approach, or point me to the right place to track this request?

You mentioned that a single payment took 3.8–4.8 seconds with 350 channels. Have you measured payment time with the smallest possible setup?
Using WebSocket subscriptions on the client to receive signing requests could significantly reduce per-payment latency. In my own tests with a minimal setup, I’m seeing around 500 ms per payment, although that’s under fairly ideal conditions.
